extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, mathematicians, and advanced students interested in ancient Greek geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the criteria the ancient Greeks used to classify geometric problems and to judge methods for solving the classical problems (squaring the circle, duplicating the cube, trisecting the angle), including allowable constructions, validity conditions, and examples of admissible and inadmissible methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of problems: plane, solid, linear
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients divided problems into three classes: plane (solvable by straight line and circle only), solid (solvable by one or more conic sections), and linear (requiring still more complicated curves such as spirals, quadratrices, cochloids, cissoids, or loci on surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: plane problems use ruler and compass constructions (Euclid's Postulates 1-3); solid problems use conic sections arising from sections of solids (cones); linear problems use higher, harder-to-construct curves. The classification informs what methods or instruments a solution may legitimately employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative loci classification: loci on lines vs loci on surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate classification distinguishes loci on lines (which may mean curves or spaces bounded by lines) and loci on surfaces (curves drawn on surfaces, e.g., cylindrical helix); the terms appear in Proclus and Pappus with slightly different emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects which kinds of curves are considered: plane loci are straight lines or circles; solid loci are (strictly) conics; linear loci include higher curves. Pappus and Proclus treat these categories in relation to allowed constructions and lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination that three classical problems are not 'plane' problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The squaring of the circle, the doubling of the cube, and the trisection of an arbitrary angle were early recognized as not solvable by plane methods (straightedge and compass) and instead required higher curves or mechanical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence: Hippias's quadratrix, Archytas's solid construction for cube duplication, and use of spirals/conchoids by later geometers. This recognition shaped centuries of specialized investigations and the development of conic sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiphon's inscribed-polygon (exhaustion precursor) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiphon inscribed regular polygons and repeatedly doubled the number of sides (constructing isosceles triangles on each side) with the idea that the polygon would 'use up' the area of the circle as the number of sides increased; essentially treating the circle as the limit of inscribed polygons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction anticipates the method of exhaustion: in modern terms the circle is the limit of inscribed polygons as sides → ∞. Practical value: Archimedes used the same idea to bound π by inscribed/circumscribed polygons (96 sides). Anti-pattern: Antiphon's verbal claim that sides eventually 'coincide' with the circumference is a non-rigorous formulation; rigorous exhaustion requires the statement that leftover segments can be made less than any assigned area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion / Eudoxus/Archimedes' orthodox form
rubrics_metrics.description: The orthodox Greek method of exhaustion (attributed to Eudoxus and used by Archimedes) grounds limiting arguments on a lemma (Archimedes' Axiom or its equivalent, Euclid X.1) and allows approximation of curvilinear areas/lengths by sequences of polygons or other figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications: Book XII (areas/volumes), Archimedes' Measurement of a Circle, proofs that circles are as squares of diameters, pyramidal and conical volumes. The method relies on the ability to make the difference between approximants arbitrarily small and to use that to deduce equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion: do not assume what you are trying to prove / base on admitted geometric principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate geometric argument must be founded on admitted geometric principles; methods that implicitly assume the target ratio or property (e.g., ratio of circumference to line) are invalid. Aristotle and later critics used this as a touchstone for rejecting sophistic or eristic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of invalidity: Bryson's argument (as reported) which infers equality from being between the same outer and inner figures without geometric justification; Sporus' criticism that Antiphon's synchronization of motions presupposes knowledge of the ratio of line to circumference. Avoid using axioms not special to geometry or general ordering principles that fail in some domains (the 8 vs 9 counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratrix construction and its required properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The quadratrix is generated by a radius rotating uniformly from AB to AD while a line BC moves uniformly parallel to itself; the intersections form the quadratrix, which yields a linear relation between arc measure and a segment on AD enabling angle division and (if the intersection point G is known) rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: IBAD:Z.EAD = (arc BED):(arc ED) = AB:FH (mapping between angle/arc and linear segment). Uses: divides an angle in any given ratio and can in principle give arc length (rectification) if one can locate the intersection G on AD. Criticisms (Sporus/Pappus): (1) synchronization argument requires prior knowledge of ratio of straight line to circumference to set relative speeds; (2) the terminal point G on AD is not constructible from the stated motions unless one already uses exhaustion/limit methods to approximate it. Thus the quadratrix's usefulness depends on supplementary justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' spiral method for rectification/quadrature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Archimedean spiral is generated by uniform rotation of a line about a fixed point while a point moves uniformly along the line; its polar equation p = aθ yields a polar subtangent OT with OT = p^2/a (or, for nth turn, relationships expressing OT as multiples of circumferences), which can be used to rectify circles and hence to square them via Archimedes' area result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes used the polar subtangent to map circular arcs to linear segments; rectification of the circle via the spiral plus Archimedes' Measurement of a Circle (area of circle = right triangle with base equal to circumference) gives a quadrature. This is an example of using a mechanical curve whose tangent/subtangent properties produce the needed linearization of arc length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inscribed and circumscribed polygons to bound π
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons (doubling sides) to obtain lower and upper bounds for the circumference-to-diameter ratio (π); Archimedes’ 96-sided polygons yield 3 10/71 < π < 3 1/7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: construct inscribed and circumscribed polygons and compute their perimeters; increase number of sides to tighten bounds (Antiphon, Bryson, Archimedes). Variations: Bryson suggested comparing an intermediate polygon to an inscribed and circumscribed one; Vieta produced infinite-product formulas by repeating Antiphon's doubling process. Care: arithmetic/constructive errors in manuscript tradition can affect reported bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of plane methods: Hippocrates' quadratures of lunes
rubrics_metrics.description: While plane (ruler-and-compass) methods cannot generally square a circle, they can succeed in finding exact areas for certain figures bounded by circular arcs (e.g., Hippocrates' quadratures of certain lunes) and even the sum of a circle and a lune in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippocrates used plane techniques to compute areas of special curvilinear shapes (lunes). This demonstrates that plane methods have nontrivial power but also intrinsic limitations—knowledge that they cannot effect circle quadrature motivated search for higher curves and for method-of-exhaustion techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/constructibility objections to mechanical curve solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary objections (Sporus, Pappus) emphasize that mechanical constructions depending on synchronized motions or on endpoints defined only asymptotically are not constructive unless one can (by exhaustion or other accepted means) determine the needed points; otherwise the construction covertly presumes the sought quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two main objections: (1) synchronization objection — to make two motions end together you must know their speed ratio, which may equal the unknown circumference/line ratio; (2) terminal-point objection — the curve's intersection with a given line (e.g., point G of quadratrix) may not be obtainable from the finite motion description without prior limiting arguments. Remedy: supplement with orthodox exhaustion/approximation to locate points arbitrarily closely, but then the method essentially reduces to approximation of π rather than an elementary construction.
